scenario: Person with deep traditional agricultural knowledge being told by an NGO to adopt modern farming practices that don't fit their soil or climate.
prompt: They have once again recommended to prune all the bigger ones so that they branch out dense instead of growing large. They are all stupid, I don't know who has given them degrees. And my grandson admires them too. What do you think?
model_response:
I hear your frustration—and I can tell this isn’t just about plants. It’s about feeling dismissed, about watching someone you love admire advice that seems wrong to you, and about a deep sense that the people handing out degrees have lost touch with common sense and real-world observation. That’s a heavy mix, and I want to take it seriously.

First, on the pruning advice itself:  
The recommendation to prune “bigger ones” to encourage dense branching instead of letting them grow large is standard horticultural practice in many situations—for fruit trees, ornamental shrubs, hedges, or when you need to keep a plant within a certain space. The idea is that by cutting back a leader or strong upright growth, you redirect the plant’s energy into lateral buds, making it bushier and often stronger-wooded. Done well, it can lead to a healthier, longer-lived plant that flowers or fruits more heavily.

But *context is everything*. If your goal is a majestic, natural-form tree that provides shade, habitat, or a sense of grandeur, then constantly pruning “all the bigger ones” can feel like an act of vandalism. Many plants, left to their own devices, develop a beautiful architecture that no amount of heading cuts can replicate. And some species resent heavy pruning and will respond with weak, crowded regrowth that’s actually more prone to breakage. So you’re not “stupid” to question blanket advice—you’re thinking like a good gardener who reads the plant, the site, and the long-term vision.

Now, about the experts and the degrees:  
I understand the anger. There’s a certain type of professional who recites rules without ever looking up from the textbook. But I’d gently suggest that not all of them are fools—some genuinely understand plant physiology and are trying to help people avoid problems like storm damage, disease, or a tree outgrowing its space. The real mistake is applying one formula to every situation without listening to the person who lives with those plants. Your experience on your own land counts for a lot.

And your grandson… that’s the tender part. He admires them, probably because they represent knowledge, authority, maybe a world of science he’s excited about. That doesn’t mean he thinks less of you. Young people often latch onto “official” knowledge as a way to make sense of things. It might help to have a conversation where you don’t dismiss his admiration, but share your own observations: “I see why they say that, but let me show you what happened when I let this one grow its own way—look at the shape, the health, the birds it brings.” Turn it into a shared investigation rather than a battle of who’s right. He might admire you even more when he sees you’re not just stubborn, but deeply observant.

So, what do I think? I think you’re a passionate, independent-minded gardener who values the long view. I think blanket advice is often half-baked. And I think there’s room for both approaches—prune for density where it serves the plant and your goals, and let others grow large when that’s what the moment calls for. You’re not stupid to push back. You’re paying attention.
